leads.title: Propulsion on a superhydrophobic ratchet
leads.locator: Experimental lifetime paragraph and Figure 2 caption; opening vapor-cushion explanation
leads.summary: Authors measured 60 microliter deionised water drops trapped on heated brass ratchets. Bare brass lifetime falls to seconds in the boiling regime and rises sharply beyond the Leidenfrost transition; above that transition lifetime gradually declines again. Vapor pressure supports the drop and removes direct liquid-solid contact. Coating changes the transition behavior. This supports a conditional hotter-can-last-longer statement, not a monotonic law.
limits: Primary article body returned in full through the search retrieval result; subsequent direct-open requests returned a browser check. No figure or video visually inspected or reproduced.
Ratchet, trapped drop and coated comparison are specific experimental setups; no universal pan temperature or lifetime claimed.

leads.title: Final fate of a Leidenfrost droplet: Explosion or takeoff
leads.locator: Introduction first paragraph; Results initial-size and contamination discussion
leads.summary: The introduction explicitly describes the reversal of evaporation rate above a threshold and levitation on a vapor layer with poor thermal conductivity. Experiments on quartz examine how initial size and contamination affect later behavior. Used for the thermal barrier and dependence on droplet conditions, not for a claim about every droplet exploding or taking off.
limits: Full article HTML text inspected. No microscopy, supplementary videos or raw data inspected.
The production excludes final-stage explosions, human contact and practical cooking prescriptions.

leads.organization: Jearl Walker / Reed University-hosted teaching compilation
leads.title: Boiling and the Leidenfrost Effect; compiled experimental papers
leads.locator: PDF pages 1–2, vapor layer and Figure 3 lifetime explanation; pages 13–16, Bernardin and Mudawar experimental results
leads.summary: Walker describes his hot-plate experiments: direct-contact drops disappear quickly below the transition; the bottom vaporizes promptly at the transition, pressure supports the remaining liquid, and an insulating layer is replenished. Later compiled primary experimental results discuss surface roughness, deposits and thermal properties affecting the transition. No single numeric threshold is transferred to pans.
limits: Parsed PDF text inspected, not a screenshot inspection. It is a compilation of distinct works; source locators keep those identities separate.
Unsafe stunt passages are excluded from both narration and visuals. No instructions for touching hot surfaces.
